title: AWS, Anthropic race to deploy army of specialized engineers key to proving AI spending will pay off
content: After spending billions building artificial intelligence , Big Tech is now spending heavily to build the human workforce needed to prove the investments are paying off. Companies are scrambling to find specialized AI engineers who can put the technology to work inside businesses. These specialists — called forward deployed engineers, or FDEs — combine advanced AI and software expertise with an understanding of how corporations operate. They could be the key humans in the loop required to turn powerful large language models into enterprise systems that can deliver measurable business results . Market concerns that the economics of the AI boom are not sustainable have intensified this week with many top AI-themed and memory-themed stocks from Dell to CoreWeave, AMD and Micron suffering significant short-term losses. Amazon Web Services has committed $1 billion to a forward-deployed engineering initiative. OpenAI has launched a deployment business backed by more than $4 billion in initial investment. Anthropic is putting $100 million into a program to train 10,000 forward-deployed engineers by the end of 2027. And Accenture and Google Cloud are building a 1,000-person forward-deployed engineering workforce. "The Street is starting to become impatient with these billions of companies who are spending on AI without getting any business outcomes," said Jeff Christian, founder of executive search firm Christian & Timbers. Working directly with customers, FDEs navigate existing technology systems, security requirements, and organizational obstacles to turn promising AI experiments into applications companies can actually use. At Caylent, an AWS consulting partner that embeds FDEs with customers, CEO Val Henderson said the role requires more than technical expertise. "The hardest thing to teach is the customer EQ, without question," she said, adding that engineers also need to understand customers and businesses, navigate organizational dynamics, and exercise judgment when projects encounter unexpected problems. Experienced talent is scarce, and developing that expertise can't happen overnight in a labor market race that recent hiring numbers suggest is accelerating. U.S. job postings for FDEs surged from fewer than 200 in 2023 to approximately 1,200 in 2025 and more than 7,300 in the first nine months of 2026, according to data from labor market analytics firm Lightcast . Median advertised salaries reached $195,456 during that period, up 40% from 2023 and more than three times the median advertised salary across all U.S. job postings. The competition extends well beyond the companies developing AI models. Consulting firms are among the biggest recruiters, reflecting demand for engineers who can help corporate clients implement the technology. Lightcast counted 872 unique FDE job postings from Deloitte and 688 from Accenture during the first nine months of 2026, followed by Google with 499 and KPMG with 447. The figures represent advertised positions, not completed hires. "Demand for forward deployed engineers is rising fast, and growing wages suggest employers are competing for a limited pool of talent," said Elena Magrini, head of global research at Lightcast. But the data also points to a potential solution. "FDE is not an entirely new role. It shares roughly half of its skills with software engineering, creating an opportunity to tap into a much broader talent pool," said Magrini. Technology companies and their corporate clients are investing in multiple ways to develop deployment expertise. AWS is building its own FDE organization, drawing on experienced engineers within Amazon and AWS while also recruiting externally. The company is starting with hundreds of engineers, according to Asa Kalavade, vice president of forward-deployed engineering at AWS. "We are investing $1 billion now because customers need this hands-on help turning their AI investments into results at speed," Kalavade said. OpenAI is pursuing a broader enterprise deployment strategy, backed by the $4 billion in initial investment and an agreement earlier this year to acquire Tomoro , an applied AI consulting and engineering firm expected to bring approximately 150 experienced FDEs and deployment specialists into the operation. Anthropic is taking a different approach, training engineers already employed by its customers and partners. Through its Claude Frontier Academy, the company aims to train 10,000 FDEs by the end of 2027. Its first residency cohorts include engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley, and Novo Nordisk. "The AI skills gap affects every customer and every partner, so it is a market problem, and Anthropic is committed to helping close it," said Steve Corfield, Anthropic's global head of business development and partnerships. Accenture and Google Cloud , meanwhile, are building a 1,000-person FDE workforce, relying partly on retraining experienced software engineers for customer-facing AI deployment work. "The reality is that experienced FDEs cannot simply be recruited at the scale clients need," said Ram Ramalingam, Accenture's FDE and software and platform engineering lead. Depending on their backgrounds, the company's FDE training and onboarding can take 30 to 90 days, Ramalingam said. He added that participants already have substantial software engineering experience; the program is designed to add specialized deployment capabilities rather than train beginners. AWS also sees an opportunity to develop expertise inside customer organizations. Kalavade said many businesses already employ capable engineers but need help learning how to move AI projects into production. AWS's FDEs work alongside those teams so customers can eventually maintain and expand the systems themselves. The challenge goes beyond technical expertise, said Corfield. "A skill in short supply is an engineer who can understand how the business works and also build the system that changes it," he said. Anthropic believes some of that expertise can be developed through structured engineering. Its Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency borrows from medical education, pairing experienced engineers with practitioners and evaluating them on realistic enterprise deployments. "We modeled the residency on how medicine trains doctors," Corfield said. Participants learn from practicing engineers, work on realistic cases, and are assessed before they practice on their own companies, according to Anthropic. They then receive 12 weeks of mentorship from Anthropic engineers while working on Claude projects. The first full credentials are expected in early 2027. According to Christian, experienced FDEs can help expand the workforce by leading teams of less-experienced engineers. For instance, he said, those who have completed 10 to 15 successful deployments may have the judgment to supervise teams of five or six, passing along expertise gained from working through complicated customer projects. Christian sees that mentorship model as a way to expand deployment teams without requiring an elite engineer in every position. But Henderson said the customer-facing judgment required for complex AI deployments is particularly difficult to teach. While technical skills can be developed through training, engineers also need experience navigating real-world customer challenges. "There is no compression algorithm for experience," Henderson said. For Christian, the challenge comes back to the pressure from investors to produce business results. He argued that companies need engineers who can work directly with customers to translate increasingly powerful AI systems into practical applications. "The only way you can get AI to work is by human-to-human interaction," he said. The ultimate test is whether this expanding workforce can help companies generate the return on investment from AI that justifies the upfront costs. To date, the available evidence from FDE projects falls short of confirmation. Some early deployments show productivity improvements but not financial returns, according to company-reported case studies. At mortgage lender PennyMac, Caylent's FDEs worked alongside product managers and engineers on an AI-enabled mortgage servicing platform. Some engineering tasks were completed as much as six times faster, depending on the task, according to a case study provided by AWS. Another Caylent engagement involved Smarsh, a communications compliance software provider. A company case study estimated that the project freed $5 million to $10 million in engineering and product capacity that could be redirected to other work. Caylent confirmed that FDEs participated in the project, although the figure does not isolate their contribution or represent equivalent cash savings. These improvements in engineering productivity and capacity are not independently verified returns on AI investment. Anthropic's ambitious training initiative has yet to demonstrate measurable results. Corfield acknowledged that it is still too early for outcome data and said the company plans to track how quickly participants' projects reach production and how extensively those systems are used.

title: Memory stocks are getting hammered. China and a 2029 oversupply are the big worries
content: Memory chip stocks have taken a particularly bad beating this week amid broader equity market turmoil. Two concerns are adding to the pressure — the debate over whether Chinese competition is threatening memory incumbents and speculation about when the market could become oversupplied. Over the last five days, SK Hynix has plunged 26%, Samsung has tanked 22% and Micron has dropped around 11%. The initial jitters came at the start of the week after China's leading memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , announced plans to roll out a server memory product based on new architecture . CXMT's design would allow higher storage density, raising concerns that the breakthrough could result in the Chinese company taking global market share from rivals Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. However, a number of analysts questioned whether CXMT would be able to scale the production of such an advanced technology. "The issue, of course, was with any architectural change ... you can make the chips, but what yield are you getting? If you're only getting a 50% yield, you're literally putting half the chips in the bin because they don't work very well," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday. Kevin Cassidy, a senior research analyst at Rosenblatt Securities, also said the developments at CXMT are unlikely to add more supply of memory onto the market. "We don't think this is going to swing the supply-demand equation at all," Cassidy told CNBC. Traders are also discussing comments from an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper , a prominent South Korean publication, in which a reporter urged the country's government to prepare for a slowdown in the AI boom and to identify and develop the next big growth engine. The writer said that two people — Professor Hwang of the Seoul National University and Ahn Ki-hyun, executive director of the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association — expect to see a "flood of new supply" that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" in 2029, according to a CNBC translation. By 2030, "the supercycle could be over and the industry could enter a downturn," the writer said. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded to the article in a post on X , saying that China "will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028." Random access memory (RAM) is produced by the likes of SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron as well as CXMT in China. An oversupply of RAM in 2029 would pose yet another headwind for memory stocks, with lower prices and a squeeze on profit margins. But a forecast that far out hasn't been echoed by other analysts. Typically, the biggest customers for memory chips have been consumer electronics companies, because memory is a key component of devices like smartphones and laptops. But with the AI boom picking up pace, memory has also become a key component of Nvidia chips and other parts of the data center supply chain. With demand increasing, supply has tightened, leading to unprecedented price rises. That has led to huge rallies in the share price of Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the three biggest memory makers. But a key question for investors is whether the industry’s typical boom-and-bust cycle is finally changing. Memory prices have traditionally surged when demand outstrips supply, only to fall as manufacturers ramp up production and the market becomes oversupplied. Investors are trying to work out if that cycle no longer exists or whether there has been a fundamental change. All of the major memory makers are currently in the process of expanding capacity, but it takes around three to five years for a factory to be built and come online. That has led many analysts to forecast that the shortage won't ease until 2028 — but that might not necessarily lead to huge price declines. Counterpoint Research sees the price of DRAM, another key type of memory, falling around 23% in 2028 compared with 2027. However, the DRAM price would still be up around 230% compared to 2025. "The current memory market is considered to be in a 'New Normal' era, and the down cycle will differ from previous ones," Jeongku Choi, senior research analyst at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC. "Suppliers and buyers enter into 3- to 5-year Long-Term Agreements (LTAs), involving substantial upfront payments and established upper and lower price limits to ensure consistency. Consequently, even if a down cycle occurs, it is not expected to show the same sharp decline seen in the past." — CNBC's Lisa Kim helped contribute to this report.

Scientists expected Zimbabwe’s fossil beds to yield familiar South African dinosaurs, but the newly named Musango is helping reveal a distinct prehistoric community. Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth’s animal and plant species . This diversity is driven by diverse habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines, and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for nearly two centuries . Africa is most famous for spectacular hominid fossils that reveal our own ancestry. However, the continent boasts many fabulous fossil finds, including those of the most familiar extinct animals – dinosaurs. The first African dinosaur fossils to be noted scientifically hailed from the Eastern Cape, South Africa, and were described in the 1850s. Since then, the African dinosaur map has expanded, with rich fossil beds in South Africa, Lesotho, Tanzania, Egypt, Niger, Malawi, Madagascar, and Morocco. Zimbabwe is an important part of the African dinosaur puzzle, with dinosaur bones reported since 1916 . As a specialist on early dinosaurs who has worked on similar material from China, the UK and Africa, I’ve been drawn to these Zimbabwean fossils to see what they reveal about the first stages of their evolution. Our latest addition to the Triassic zoo, Musango matusadonaensis , is a sauropodomorph dinosaur. (That’s the dinosaur subgroup that eventually gave rise to four-legged, long-necked giants like Diplodocus .) Its incomplete skeleton was found in the bank of the Nyamasango River close to Musango Island, as captured in the animal’s scientific name. Musango ’s anatomy shows us that it was bipedal (walking on its hind legs only), reached about 4.5 meters in length, and weighed 220 kg. Growth marks in its bones reveal that it was a subadult when it died. Sadly, the skull wasn’t preserved, so its diet is unknown, but its close relatives were largely herbivorous (plant-eating). Our new work reveals something unexpected about Zimbabwean dinosaurs. They’re not simply an extension of better-known South African faunas but include an array of species unique to the region. We’re now trying to work out why these differences exist. We suspect that environmental conditions might be the key. Early fossil finds in Zimbabwe were overlooked by many scientists, and it was not until the 1970s that they became more generally known . This was thanks to pioneering work by Zimbabwean paleontologists Geoffrey Bond and Michael Raath, who discovered abundant material in the hinterlands of Bulawayo (south-west Zimbabwe) and the lower Zambezi Valley (forming the border with Zambia). Most of these finds were identified as belonging to known species named from neighboring South Africa. Palaeontological work in Zimbabwe stalled for a few decades. However, a band of devoted fossil hunters kept searching. One of them, Steve Edwards, a local safari camp manager, found new, productive sites on the shore of Lake Kariba, the artificial lake which forms most of the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia. News of the discoveries eventually reached Jonah Choiniere at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg. Jonah, an expert on early dinosaurs, immediately recognized the importance of the material. He assembled an international team of South African, Zimbabwean, and UK-based collaborators to explore them further. This was a major task, as the sites on Late Kariba’s shoreline are deep inside Matusadona National Park. Our solution was to use one of the Kariba houseboats as a mobile hotel and laboratory, so that we could prospect the shoreline. We mounted two expeditions, in 2017 and 2018. We have been cleaning and studying this material ever since. Both trips yielded a trove of material, collected from brick-red mudstones and sandstones that were laid down by ancient rivers around 210 million years ago, during the Late Triassic period (237-201 million years ago) . Geological evidence and plant fossils show that the Triassic landscape of Kariba was dry and dotted with stands of large conifer trees, with green corridors of vegetation following permanent watercourses. Sauropodomorphs are the most common Late Triassic dinosaurs. But what’s interesting about Musango and its relative Musankwa (which we described from the same beds in 2024) is that they are unique to Zimbabwe. We’d expected to find South African dinosaur species in these beds, given their similar age and geographic proximity, but surprisingly all the material we’ve collected so far has revealed animals that are distinct from those elsewhere. These Zimbabwean dinosaurs are not even the closest relatives of their South African neighbors. We’ve also found other fossil animals, including lungfish and aquatic reptiles called phytosaurs, which are rare or absent in South African sites. Following this, we’ve started to reappraise the historical dinosaur collections in Bulawayo. It appears that many of these fossils can’t be referred to South African species either, contrary to earlier assumptions. Then, as now, Zimbabwe was further north than South Africa and closer to the equator, so climatic differences might be responsible for these varied casts of characters (as climate is known to have a strong effect on the distributions of living animals). To probe this further, we’ll be going back to Kariba in search of more fossils. We’ll also collect more information on the exact ages and environments of these dinosaur-bearing rocks, to compare them more precisely with sites elsewhere. Although the significance of these dinosaurs is only just coming to light, Zimbabwe is already taking a greater role in shedding much-needed light on early dinosaur evolution.
